About: the Gamow peak: the narrow window of energies where thermonuclear fusion reactions come from

About this simulation

On screen
Left: against E/kT from 0 to 35, the Maxwell factor e−E/kT (solid), the tunnelling factor e−√(EG/E) (dashed) and their product (blue, shaded), each scaled to its own maximum on the plot; a tick marks E = kT and a thin dashed line marks E0, the peak of the product. Right: the Coulomb barrier V against r on a logarithmic energy scale, with lines at kT and E0, the classically forbidden band shaded, and a pair of energy E0 approaching and turning back at rt. Below it: the true height of the peak, e−τG, on a logarithmic scale against T for all three pairs, the selected pair bold with a dot at the current T and small dots at the temperatures already visited; the note gives the local power law, height ∝ TτG/3, and the rate exponent ζ = (τG − 2)/3.
Controls
Reaction chooses the pair of nuclei (charges, mass numbers and reduced mass). Temperature sets T from 1.0 to 3.0 × 107 K; the curves and readouts follow the slider continuously.
Measured
kT, E0 and Vn in keV; E0/kT; the true height of the product at E0, e−τG with τG = 3E0/kBT, given as a power of ten. All of these are in the sidebar Readouts. The S-factor is left out; the barrier is Coulomb down to rn = 1.2(A11/3 + A21/3) fm.
Conditions
Non-resonant reactions with a constant nuclear factor S, a Maxwell–Boltzmann gas and a bare Coulomb barrier (no electron screening). The heights compare Gamow factors only: a real rate also carries S, which for p + p, a weak-interaction reaction, is some twenty powers of ten smaller than for p + 14N. The peak is close to Gaussian, with 1/e half-width 2(E0kBT/3)1/2.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Where the reactions come from

Choose the reaction p + p and set the temperature to 1.6 × 107 K, about the temperature at the centre of the Sun. Before looking at the blue product curve, predict where it has its peak.

2 · The peak and the barrier

Keep the settings of question 1. Before reading the inset, predict how the energy E0 of the peak compares with the height Vn of the Coulomb barrier.

3 · Switching to nitrogen

Keep the temperature at 1.6 × 107 K. Predict what happens to the peak when the reaction is switched to p + 14N; then switch it and check.

4 · Warming the nitrogen reaction

Keep the reaction p + 14N and raise the temperature from 1.6 to 2.4 × 107 K, an increase of one half. Before moving the slider, predict how the true height of the peak changes.

5 · Warming the proton reaction

Switch the reaction to p + p and make the same change, from 1.6 to 2.4 × 107 K. Before moving the slider, predict how the rise compares with the one for p + 14N.

6 · Where fusion happens

Reactions come from a narrow window of energies, the Gamow peak, at E0 = (EG(kBT)2/4)1/3: several times kBT, yet far below the Coulomb barrier, which the pairs cross only by tunnelling. The larger the charges, the further out and the lower the peak, and the more steeply its height rises with T, roughly as TE0/kBT. That is why the p–p chain runs in the Sun, while reactions on carbon and nitrogen need hotter cores.

The heights here are the Gamow factors alone. A real rate also carries each reaction's nuclear factor S: for p + p, which needs a weak decay during the brief encounter, it is some twenty powers of ten smaller than for p + 14N.

Which Pairs of Nuclei Fuse

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

Fusion in a star needs two nuclei to come close, but they repel each other. This sim shows which pair energies the reactions actually come from, for three pairs of nuclei, and how the temperature changes that.

What you'll learn

  • How the Maxwell and tunnelling factors combine into one peak.
  • How the energy of that peak compares with kBT and with the Coulomb barrier.
  • How the peak depends on the charges of the nuclei.
  • How the height of the peak depends on temperature.
The three plots. Left, the factors against E/kBT; right, the barrier and the true height.

What's on screen

  • Left, black curves: the Maxwell factor (solid) and the tunnelling factor (dashed), against E/kBT from 0 to 35. A tick marks E = kBT.
  • Blue shaded curve: their product, with a thin dashed line at its peak E0. Each curve is scaled to its own maximum.
  • Right, top: the Coulomb barrier V against r, with the forbidden band shaded red and a blue dot moving in and out. Right, bottom: the true height of the peak against T.
  • Readouts: kBT, peak E0, barrier Vn, E0/kBT and true height.
See itLook at the opening setting, p + p at 1.6 × 107 K, about the temperature at the centre of the Sun. Watch for: the left plot filling with curves, and a blue dot sliding in and out on the barrier plot.

03

Two opposing factors make one narrow peak

The rate at which two kinds of nucleus react is an average over the Maxwell distribution of their relative energy E. The notes' (4.57) shows what is averaged:

The notes' (4.57), prefactor dropped. S(E) holds the nuclear physics, varies slowly, and is left out of the sim.

The Maxwell factor falls as E rises: few pairs have a large energy. The tunnelling factor rises: the higher the energy, the likelier a pair gets through the barrier. EG is the Gamow energy, set by the charges and masses (section 05).

p + p at 1.6 × 107 K. Each curve is scaled to its own maximum, as in the notes' Figure 50.

The product is largest where E/kBT + √(EG/E) is smallest, at E0 (4.58). For p + p at 1.6 × 107 K the readouts give kBT = 1.379 keV and E0 = 6.17 keV, so E0 = 4.47 kBT.

The notes' (4.58).
Key idea. Reactions come neither from the commonest pairs nor from the likeliest tunnellers, but from a narrow window of energy between them.
See itLook at the left plot for p + p at 1.6 × 107 K. Watch for: the blue peak, with the dashed E0 line a little under five times the kBT tick, and E0/kBT reading 4.47.
04

The peak sits far below the Coulomb barrier

Two nuclei repel until they almost touch. The sim puts the barrier top at the touching separation rn = 1.2 (A11/3 + A21/3) fm, and a pair of energy E turns back where V(r) = E, at the classical turning point rt.

Z1, Z2 are the charges in units of e. Vn is V at r = rn.

For two protons rn = 2.4 fm and Vn = 600 keV. The peak energy E0 = 6.17 keV is 97 times smaller, so a pair at E0 turns back at rt = 234 fm, 97 times further out than rn. Between them lies the shaded band, closed to the pair classically. It crosses only by tunnelling, with probability about exp(−√(EG/E)) (4.53).

p + p at 1.6 × 107 K. The vertical axis is logarithmic.
Key idea. The reacting pairs have about a hundredth of the energy needed to reach the barrier top. Tunnelling does the rest.
See itOpen the Readouts and watch the blue dot on the barrier plot. Watch for: the dot coming in from the right along the E0 line and turning back at about 234 fm, while the barrier top, 600 keV, stands far above it at the left.
05

Larger charges push the peak out and lower it

EG grows with the charges and the reduced mass μr (4.53):

The notes' (4.53). Z1Z2 = 1, 4 and 7 for the three pairs.

EG is 0.49 MeV for p + p, 23.6 MeV for ³He + ³He and 45.1 MeV for p + ¹⁴N, about 91 times that of p + p. A bigger EG puts the peak at more multiples of kBT, where far fewer pairs have the energy.

Each product curve is scaled to its own maximum, so the plot shows where the peak sits, not how high it is.

At 1.6 × 107 K the peak is at 4.5, 16.2 and 20.1 kBT, and its true height, e−τG, falls from 10−5.8 to 10−21.2 and 10−26.2. The heights compare Gamow factors only: a real rate also carries S, which differs between reactions.

Key idea. More charge means a higher barrier to tunnel, so the reactions come from rarer, more energetic pairs.
See itSwitch to ³He + ³He at the same temperature. Watch for: the peak moving out to about 16 times the kBT tick, and the true height reading 10−21.2.
See itNow switch to p + ¹⁴N. Watch for: the peak moving further out, to about 20 kBT, and the true height reading 10−26.2.
06

A small rise in temperature lifts the height a lot

The height e−τG depends on T only through τG, which falls slowly as T rises. But τG is a large exponent, so a small change in it moves the height a lot.

The notes' (4.59). The sim shows τG as 3 × E0/kBT.

Near a given T this is a power law: height ∝ TτG/3, and τG/3 = E0/kBT. The rate also carries a factor T−2/3, so it goes as Tζ with ζ = (τG − 2)/3 (4.64):

The notes' (4.63) and (4.64). At 1.6 × 107 K, ζ is 3.8 for p + p and 19.5 for p + ¹⁴N.
T

This slider moves the sim too.

Raising T by half, from 1.6 to 2.4 × 107 K, lifts the height for p + ¹⁴N from 10−26.2 to 10−22.9, about two thousand times. For p + p it goes from 10−5.8 to 10−5.1, about five times.

Key idea. The larger τG is, the more steeply the rate climbs with temperature.
See itWarm p + ¹⁴N from 1.6 to 2.4 × 107 K. Watch for: the true height climbing from 10−26.2 to 10−22.9, and the small dots on the bottom plot marking each temperature passed.
See itMake the same warming for p + p. Watch for: the true height moving only from 10−5.8 to 10−5.1.
07

Where it matters, from the Sun to massive stars

  • The Sun's core. At about 1.6 × 107 K two protons react at E0 ≈ 6 keV, four to five kBT, tunnelling a barrier about a hundred times higher. The proton–proton chain supplies nearly all the Sun's energy.
  • The CNO cycle. Each proton capture meets a barrier of six or seven protons, and the Gamow energies are 65 to 90 times that of p + p. Near the Sun's centre εCNO ∝ T20 against εpp ∝ T4, so the CNO cycle overtakes at about 2 × 107 K, in stars somewhat more massive than the Sun.
  • Convective cores. A rate this steep concentrates the energy release near the centre, which is why more massive main-sequence stars have convective cores.
Go deeper: the width of the peak

Near E0 the product is close to a Gaussian that falls to 1/e of its peak at a distance 2√(E0kBT/3) on either side (4.59). For p + p at 1.6 × 107 K that is 3.4 keV, a little over half of E0, so most reactions come from about 3 to 10 keV.

08

Summary

In one line. This sim shows which pair energies fusion comes from, and how that depends on the nuclei and on the temperature.
  • Reactions come from a narrow peak, E0 = (EG(kBT)²/4)1/3, at several kBT and far below Vn.
  • A larger Z1Z2 moves the peak out and lowers it.
  • The true height e−τG rises as TτG/3 near a given T; τG = 3E0/kBT.

Common mix-ups

  • "Fusion uses the typical pair, at about kBT." For p + p the peak is at 4.5 kBT, and for p + ¹⁴N at 20 kBT.
  • "A pair must reach the top of the barrier." E0 is 6.17 keV against 600 keV; the pair tunnels the rest.
  • "A slightly hotter gas barely changes a slow reaction." For p + ¹⁴N, a rise of one half in T lifts the height about two thousand times.

Things to try on your own

  • Choose ³He + ³He and drag T from 1.0 to 3.0 × 107 K. Read how E0/kBT changes.
  • Set p + ¹⁴N to 3.0 × 107 K and compare its true height with ³He + ³He at 1.6 × 107 K.
